This specific occurrence of the letter "o" in the middle of compounds (samāsa) and derivatives (taddhita) is a characteristic of the Manogaṇa. The formation of the accusative case by changing it to "o," as in "vaco sutvā (having heard the word), siro chindi (cut the head), ayo kantati (cuts iron)," is also a characteristic of the Manogaṇa.

The method described for the Manogaṇa is not found in the feminine gender; it is found appropriately only in the masculine and neuter genders. Thus, in every way, forms ending in -sā, -so, -si, forms with the letter "o" in the middle of compounds and derivatives, and forms ending in "o" in the accusative case are evident in the Manogaṇa. This is the characteristic of the Manogaṇa. Thus, the clear characteristic of the Manogaṇa, free from confusion and complexity, has been well explained.

Now, we shall speak of the characteristics of the Manogaṇādi. Those words which appropriately end in -sā, -so, -si in the instrumental, genitive, and locative cases, but do not have the letter "o" at the end (middle) of compounds and derivatives.
159:
When these words are associated with a verb, they do not take forms ending in the letter 'o' in the accusative case. All such words should be understood as the 'Manogaṇādi group'.

For example: bila (hole), pada (foot), mukha (face/mouth), etc. Their forms are: bilasā (by the hole), bilaso (of the hole), bilasi (in the hole), bilagato (gone to the hole), bilaṃ pāvisi (entered the hole). Padasāva agamāsi (went by foot only), tīṇi padavārāni (three steps), mākāsi mukhasā pāpaṃ (do not commit evil with the mouth), mukhagataṃ bhojanaṃ chaḍḍāpeti (causes the food in the mouth to be vomited). Saccena danto damasā upeto (tamed by truth, endowed with self-control). Rasavaraṃ rasamayaṃ rasaṃ pivi (drank the excellent taste, made of taste, the taste). This is the characteristic of the Manogaṇādi group.

There is also another characteristic of the Manogaṇādi group. Although certain words have the letter 'o' in the middle in compounds and so forth, they do not take forms ending in 'sā, so, si' in the nā, sa, and smiṃ cases. Furthermore, when associated with a verb, they do not take forms ending in the letter 'o' in the accusative case. These words are also to be understood as the 'Manogaṇādi group'.

For example: āpo (water), vāyo (air), sarado (autumn/year), etc. Their forms are: āpodhātu, vāyodhātu, āpokasiṇaṃ, vāyokasiṇaṃ, āpomayaṃ, vāyomayaṃ, jīva tvaṃ saradosataṃ (may you live for a hundred years), saradakālo (autumn time). In the declension of cases: āpena, āpassa, āpe, āpasmiṃ, āpamhi. Vāyena, vāyassa, vāye, vāyasmiṃ, vāyamhi. Saradena, saradassa, sarade, saradasmiṃ, saradamhi. Āpaṃ āpato sañjānāti (perceives water as water). Vāyaṃ vāyato sañjānāti (perceives air as air). Saradaṃ pattheti (longs for autumn), saradaṃ ramaṇīyā nadī (the river is delightful throughout the autumn).
160:
In this regard, some might say, "In the Dispensation, should not the word vāyu be desired in the Manogaṇādi group, just like the word vāya?" To this, I shall reply—

Between those two words, "vāyu" and "vāyo", only the latter word "vāyo" is desired in the Manogaṇādi group. The initial word "vāyu", however, is not desired in this Manogaṇādi group by virtue of taking only words with similar 'a' endings.

Indeed, words such as "manodhātu" and "vāyodhātu" are formed with the letter 'o' in the middle only by virtue of being 'a' endings. If the word "vāyu" were taken in this Manogaṇādi group, the form "vāyodhātu" with the letter 'o' in the middle would not be possible.

To clarify this point: just as the form "āyusā" with the letter 's' appears in the Metta Sutta as "āyusā ekaputtaṃ", similar to words like "manasā", the form of the word "vāyu" with the letter 's' is not evident. Therefore, there is no place for that word "vāyu" in the Manogaṇādi group.

This being so, teachers have explained the meaning of the word "vāyodhātu" in various texts as "it blows, therefore it is called vāyo". In the verse "Where earth, water, fire, and air do not gain a footing", the triad of words beginning with "āpo" belongs to the Manogaṇādi group.

This too is a characteristic of the Manogaṇādi group. In this context, the Manogaṇādi group is divided into two: those beginning with "bila" and "pada", and those beginning with "āpo". Thus, the characteristic of the Manogaṇādi group has been well presented without confusion, without obstruction, and without complexity.

## Characteristics of the Amanogaṇa

Next, I shall describe the characteristics of the Amanogaṇa (non-manas group):

Those words which end in 'so' in the context of the nā-case, and also end in 'so' in the context of the smā-case—such words that share these endings are known as 'Amanogaṇa'.
161:
What are those words? They are words such as attha, vyañjana, akkhara, sadda, etc., as well as the words dīgha and ora. Among them, in the context of the nā-case for words like attha, there are forms ending in 'so' such as "atthaso, vyañjanaso, akkharaso, suttaso, upāyaso, sabbaso, thānaso", and so on. For the words dīgha and ora, in the context of the smā-case, there are forms ending in 'so' such as "dīghaso" and "oraso". This is the characteristic of the Amanogaṇa.

There is also another characteristic:

Those words which are entirely free from the states of ending in 'sā', 'so', 'syanta', and so forth—such words that are free from these various endings are also known as 'Amanogaṇa'.

What are those words? They are "puriso, kaññā, cittaṃ", and so forth. This too is a characteristic of the Amanogaṇa. Thus, the characteristic of the Amanogaṇa has been well presented without confusion, without obstruction, and without complexity.

When the characteristics of the Manogaṇa and so forth have been thus shown, someone might say: "You have stated the characteristic of the Manogaṇādi group with words like 'those which have the letter o in the middle in compounds, etc.' Because of that statement, words like go and para in 'parosataṃ, gomayaṃ, godhano', etc., also fall into the Manogaṇādi group." They do not. If you ask why:

In this characteristic, the statement 'having the letter o in the middle' is made based on the transformation of the final vowel of the Manogaṇādi words into 'o'. It is not stated based on augments (āgama) and so forth. In 'parosataṃ, gomayaṃ', etc., the preceding words 'para' and 'go' are only Amanogaṇa. This is because the 'o' in 'paro' is due to being an augment and due to its irregularity.

Therefore, they do not fall into the Manogaṇādi group. Thus, the characteristic of the Amanogaṇa has been shown in its entirety in every way. In this manner, in the explanation of the Manogaṇa, it should be understood that there are three divisions: the Manogaṇa, the Manogaṇādi group, and the Amanogaṇa.
162: Among those three varieties, when words belonging to the Manogaṇa group enter into a compound (samāsa), they take various forms according to the three genders, such as: "avyaggamanaso naro" (a man with an undistracted mind), "thiracetasaṃ kulaṃ" (a family with a firm mind), and "saddheyyavacasaā upāsikā" (a female lay devotee with believable words). Regarding this matter of compounds, some teachers say: "When the word 'mana' does not occur in its own sense of 'mind' but occurs in another sense (aññattha), such as 'He who has an undistracted mind is called avyaggamanaso' or 'He who has an undaunted mind is called alīnamanaso,' then the paradigm (padamālā) is obtained only according to the purisa-method, and not according to the manogaṇa-method." Their statement should not be accepted because both the purisa-method and the manogaṇa-method can be obtained as appropriate. Indeed, this is true; in the Visuddhimagga, with reference to a person, it is seen in the manogaṇa-method (as 'cetaso') in the passage: "...having accepted the request (of the Venerable Saṅghapāla) whose mind (cetaso) was adorned with virtues such as patience, composure, and loving-kindness." Also in the commentary (Ṭīkā) of that Visuddhimagga, the manogaṇa-method (as 'cetasa') is seen: "...being requested by the Elder Dāṭhānāga who had a firm mind (thiracetasā)." Therefore, the statement of those teachers should not be accepted. Those who speak thus, thinking with a confused intellect that words like 'avyaggamanasa' should be established as basic forms ending in the letter 'sa' (as 'avyaggamanasa-'), believe they should be declined according to the purisa-method in all cases and both numbers. If this were so, the forms for the sixth, fourth, and third cases such as "guṇabhūsitacetaso" and "thiracetasā" would be destroyed, and other undesired forms would arise. Because such [errors] could occur, one should not accept their view but should note the following distinction: In a context where, by the power of a compound, words like 'mana' and 'cetas' do not occur in their own sense but in another sense (aññattha), the paradigm of those words that have the 's' augment (sakārāgama) is obtained according to both the purisa-method and the manogaṇa-method as appropriate. However, the paradigm of those words without the 's' augment is obtained only according to the purisa-method. In a context of a compound where words like 'mana' occur in their own sense, the paradigm of those words like 'mana' without the 's' augment is obtained according to both the purisa-method and the manogaṇa-method.
163:
Now, to clarify this meaning and to produce expertise in the nature of words for the wise, I shall demonstrate the paradigm (padamālā) of the aforementioned words by dividing them into three types. Firstly, for this word which strictly refers to a person: "He who has a mind attached to various objects is called vyāsattamanaso." Its paradigm is as follows:

Vyāsattamanaso naro, vyāsattamanasā narā. Vyāsattamanasaṃ naraṃ, vyāsattamanase nare. Vyāsattamanasā, vyāsattamanena narena, vyāsattamanehi, vyāsattamanebhi narehi. Vyāsattamanaso, vyāsattamanassa narassa, vyāsattamanānaṃ narānaṃ. Vyāsattamanasā, vyāsattamanasmā, vyāsattamanamhā narā, vyāsattamanehi, vyāsattamanebhi narehi. Vyāsattamanaso, vyāsattamanassa narassa, vyāsattamanānaṃ narānaṃ. Vyāsattamanasi, vyāsattamane, vyāsattamanasmiṃ, vyāsattamanami nare, vyāsattamanesu naresu. Bho vyāsattamanasa nara, bhavanto vyāsattamanasā narā. Thus is the paradigm.

In this way, the presence or absence of the 's' augment (sakārāgama) should be determined. In this paradigm, the 's' augment occurs as appropriate in the singular and plural of the first and second cases, and in the singular of the third, fourth, sixth, and seventh cases, because they are followed by substituted vowels or inflectional vowels. This method is subtle and should be well-noted.

Another method: For this word which also refers to a person, "He who has a mind attached to various objects is called vyāsattamano," the paradigm follows the purisa-method as: "vyāsattamano naro, vyāsattamanā narā, vyāsattamanaṃ naraṃ," and so on. In this method, however, the 's' augment does not occur in any place.

Yet another method: For this word which refers to the mind itself, "That which is attached to various objects and is also a mind is vyāsattamano," the paradigm follows the mana-method in the manogaṇa group as: "vyāsattamano, vyāsattamanā; vyāsattamanaṃ, vyāsattamane; vyāsattamanasā, vyāsattamanena," and so on. In this method...
164:
The 's' augment occurs only in the singular of the third, fourth, sixth, and seventh cases because it is followed by a substituted vowel. Just as in this word, this three-fold method should also be understood for words like "alīnamanaso naro."

When used in the neuter gender, the paradigm should be applied as: "vyāsattamanasaṃ kulaṃ, vyāsattamanānī kulāni; vyāsattamanasaṃ kulaṃ, vyāsattamanānī kulāni; vyāsattamanasā kulena," and so on. Here, the 's' augment occurs as appropriate only in the singular of the first, second, third, fourth, sixth, and seventh cases because it is followed by substituted vowels or inflectional vowels. This method is also subtle and should be well-noted.

When used in the feminine gender, the 's' augment is used only in the nominative singular as "vyāsattamanasā itthī," and thereafter it should be declined according to the kaññā-method as: "vyāsattamanā, vyāsattamanāyo itthiyo; vyāsattamanaṃ itthiṃ." It is also the same for: "saddheyyavacasaā upāsikā, saddheyyavacāyo upāsikāyo; saddheyyavacaṃ upāsikaṃ." However, as in "vyāsattamanaṃ kulaṃ, vyāsattamanā itthī," they should be declined according to the citta-method and kaññā-method respectively. In this case, the 's' augment does not occur in any place.

To generate analytical knowledge in the listeners, I shall show other paradigms along with their derivatives: The mind itself is 'mānasa'; he who has a well-exerted mind is 'samussāhitamānaso.' It should be declined according to the purisa-method: "samussāhitamānaso, samussāhitamānasā; samussāhitamānasaṃ, samussāhitamānase; samussāhitamānasena." He who has good wisdom is 'sumedhaso.' It is declined according to the purisa-method: "sumedhaso, sumedhasā; sumedhasaṃ, sumedhase; sumedhasena." It is the same for "bhūrimedhaso" and others. In that regard, these are the usages:

Bāvarī the Brahmin asked: "Pingiya, why do you stay away even for a moment from that Gotama, who is of great wisdom (bhūrimedhasā), who is of good wisdom (sumedhasā)?" Pingiya replied: "Uncle Bāvarī, I do not stay away even for a moment from that Gotama, who is of great wisdom (bhūrimedhasā), who is of good wisdom (sumedhasā)."

In the feminine gender, forms like "samussāhitamānasā" and "sumedhasā" should be used, and in the neuter gender, forms like "samussāhitamānasaṃ" and "sumedhasaṃ" should be used. The paradigms of these words should be applied according to the kaññā-method and citta-method. The determination of the feminine gender and others in the place of masculine words ending in 'o' is made to demonstrate the various methods. In truth, in this text, only the mention of words ending in 'o' is intended. Furthermore, in the world, that which is called Nīti...
165:
“The Exalted Gotama, who possesses wisdom as vast as the earth and is endowed with excellent wisdom, is called ‘Sumedha’. Pingiya, why do you remain apart from that Exalted Gotama even for a moment?

The Exalted Gotama possesses wisdom as vast as the earth; the Exalted Gotama possesses wisdom as vast as the earth. Brahman, I do not remain apart from that Exalted Gotama, who possesses wisdom as vast as the earth, even for a moment.”

When expressed in the feminine gender, the forms ‘samussāhitamānasā sumedhasā’ occur; when expressed in the neuter gender, the forms ‘samussāhitamānasam sumedhasam’ occur. The declension (padamālā) of these words should be applied according to the method of ‘kaññā’ and ‘citta’. The determination of feminine gender and so on in the context of masculine nouns ending in ‘o’ (o-kāranta) is made for the purpose of illustrating the method. Specifically, it is the discussion of words ending in ‘o’ that is intended here. Furthermore, in the world, what is known as ‘nīti’ (guidance/grammar) is beautiful only when explained through various methods; and since this work is a ‘nīti’ within the Sasana, it should be noted that it is explained through various methods.

All these words ending in ‘o’,
Have been declared as masculine by way of method,
For the benefit of the Great Sage’s Sasana.
Among those words, whatever distinction is evident,
In the place of the nominative case (paṭhamā vibhatti) in some Pali,
I shall now explain that distinction.

By the method of “vanappagumbe yatha phussitagge” and so on, in some Pali, masculine forms ending in ‘o’ may appear in another form (ending in ‘e’). That form should also be shown as the nominative case only. Some teachers say, “In the place of the nominative case, it is shown by the locative (sattamī).”

I shall show some sutta terms in that distinction—there is no self-action (attakāre), there is no other-action (parakāre), there is no human-action (purisakāre), saṃsāra is limited (pariyantakate saṃsāre), the soul is the seventh (jīve sattame), it should not be said thus, both fools (bāle) and the wise (paṇḍite) will wander and cycle through saṃsāra and make an end of suffering.
166:
These (sutta terms) should be understood in two ways: by way of the singular and the plural. The substitution of the letter ‘e’ in the nominative singular and plural should also be known.

Those who say, “‘vanappagumbe’ is an indication of the locative case (bhummavacana-niddesa) for the nominative case,” should be asked: “If ‘vanappagumbe’ is an indication of the locative for the nominative, then since the sense of a location (ādhāra) can be heard as in the example ‘He cooks rice in a pot (thāliyaṃ)’, what meaning does this phrase ‘In the first summer month of the summer months (gimhāna māse paṭhamasmiṃ gimhe)’ illustrate?” They might reply, “O Teacher, we do not say that this word ‘vanappagumbe’ is the locative case; rather, we say it is the indication of the nominative case by the locative form.” Even if you say so, you are still at fault. In the example, “Gotamī, give to the Sangha (saṅghe),” even if it is said that the dative case (sampadāna) is indicated by the locative, because the Sangha is the location for the act of giving, those who hear the word “saṅghe” certainly experience both the hearing of a location and the conception of a location, do they not?

This is because it is not possible to prevent the mind that arises in this way. Therefore, in this matter, only this distinction should be accepted: “The form of the nominative case also sometimes occurs like the form of the locative case.” If accepted in this way, there is no contradiction. For in such places, why would the Blessed One—who is skilled in the various linguistic forms and compassionate toward all beings—if the nominative case were to be indicated, not indicate it as such, but instead use a locative indication as if to cause confusion among people? Therefore, one should not say “locative indication” merely by taking a slight hint of phonetic similarity. If you desire a locative indication by taking phonetic similarity, you should also desire “the indication of the nominative singular by the accusative plural (upayoga-bahuvacana).”

Furthermore, in the same way, if there is a locative indication for the nominative in the word “attakāre,” because the hearing of a location is possible, the unintended meaning “In self-action, there is no object” would result, rather than the intended meaning “Self-action does not exist.” Even in taking it as “an indication by the accusative plural,” the meaning of the accusative...
167:
Because the (accusative meaning) cannot be expressed by the word “natthi,” it would only result in the fault of incongruity. However, just as with words like “atthi,” the word “natthi” is also associated with the nominative case; therefore, it is understood that this word “attakāre” is indeed the nominative case. 

In the passage, “Both fools (bāle) and the wise (paṇḍite) will run and wander through saṃsāra and make an end of suffering,” if one assumes the nominative is “indicated by the locative” or “indicated by the accusative,” it would be the fault of not knowing how to say even this much: “bālā ca paṇḍitā ca.” However, because of the association with the verb “karissanti” (they will make), it is understood that the words “bāle ca” and so on are indeed the nominative case.

For example, in the phrase “The eye arose (cakkhuṃ udapādi),” which is uttered by way of the augment of the niggahīta, although the nominative case is phonetically identical to the accusative case in the phrase “Give me the eye (cakkhuṃ) when asked,” the meaning of the nominative case alone appears to the listener because it is expressed by the verb “udapādi” (arose). The meaning of the accusative case, which would be a case-distortion, does not appear to the listener because it cannot be expressed by the verb “udapādi.” For when the Blessed One said, “cakkhuṃ udapādi,” who would change the word “cakkhuṃ udapādi” (into an accusative) to explain its meaning?

Similarly, although the nominative forms “bāle paṇḍite” and so on are phonetically identical to other locative and accusative forms like “bāle paṇḍite,” only the meaning of the nominative case appears to the listener. The meaning of the other cases does not appear, because the meaning must be taken according to the usage (context). Thus, the pure nominative status of words such as “vanappagumbe, bāle, paṇḍite” should be believed in essence. Their status as locative or accusative should not be believed (in essence) merely due to phonetic similarity.

As for what the Teacher (Buddhaghosa) said in the Jātaka Commentary:

“Brahman, I desire the three mountains (three kingdoms),
And the Pañcāla, Kuru, and Kekaka kingdoms between them.
Brahman, I desire even more than that.
O Brahman, heal me who am led by desire (kāmanītaṃ).”
168:
In the commentary on this Kāmanīta Jātaka, it is stated that the word "Kekake" is an Accusative case used in the place of the Nominative case, and by that word, the kingdom of King Kekaka is shown. The commentator who says this likely speaks with the intention of the commonly occurring meaning, thinking, "This word also has the nature of the Accusative plural," because in phrases such as "purise passati," "purise patiṭṭhitaṃ," and "passāmi loke sadhane manusse," the words "purise, loke, sadhane, manusse," etc., usually appear as Accusative plural or Locative singular, and their status as Nominative singular or plural is not prominent. Indeed, teachers sometimes explain separately according to their own preference in certain places.

Regarding this word "Kekake," our preference is as follows: This word is only the Nominative case, like the appositional words "Pañcālā" and "Kuruyo." Because it refers to a kingdom, it is spoken in the plural form like the word "Kuruyo." For the Blessed One would not indicate the last word as an Accusative case among appositional words that should be indicated with identical case endings, as in "khattiyo, brāhmaṇo, vesso," etc. Furthermore, there is no logical reason to use the Accusative case "Kekake" after having spoken the Nominative cases "Pañcālā" and "Kuruyo." Therefore, this word "Kekake" is only the Nominative case.

To demonstrate this, the teacher who composed the Sandhivisodhana treatise, wishing to clarify only the Nominative case status of such words, stated in the treatise he himself composed: "Vanappagumbo vanappagumbe, sukhaṃ dukkhaṃ jīvo, sukhe dukkhe jīve." In the sub-commentary (ṭīkā) of that treatise, also clarifying only the Nominative case status of those words, he established the completed forms "vanappagumbo, sukhaṃ, dukkhaṃ, jīvo," and then stated the derived forms "vanappagumbe, sukhe, dukke, jīve" by means of the elision of the niggahīta and the substitution of the letters 'a' and 'o' with the letter 'e'. That method of derivation is in accordance with the method of the Pali Canon. The teacher Kaccāyana also, relying on the method of the Pali Canon, stated the Nominative plural word "dvipade tulyādhikaraṇe." Therefore, it is said in the Vutti: "dve padāni tulyādhikaraṇāni." "Dvipade..."
169:
Some teachers, however, desire the Locative singular status for those words (such as dvipade). Among those words, if the word 'vanappagumbe' were the Locative case (bhumma) in the place of the Nominative case (paccatta), and the word 'kekake' were also the Accusative case (upayoga) in the place of the Nominative case; then in this (Kathāvatthu Pali) passage 'esethese eke ekatṭhe,' these words 'esethese' would also be either Locative cases or Accusative cases in the place of the Nominative case. Just as those words are not of such types (Locative or Accusative) but are only pure Nominative cases, likewise, the words 'vanappagumbe, kekake,' etc., are also not of such types but are only pure Nominative cases.

Thus, in every way, it must be accepted without fail that the derivation of many words existing in the noble Sasana—such as 'vanappagumbe, bāle, paṇḍite, kekake' and 'viratte kosiyāyane, aṭṭha nāgāvāsasate, ke purise, esethese'—by way of Masculine, Feminine, Neuter genders, Pronouns, Singular, and Plural, occurs only by the substitution of the letter 'e' for the Nominative singular and plural. This pure Nominative status of words such as 'vanappagumbe, bāle, paṇḍite,' etc., is extremely subtle and difficult to understand. A clansman (kulaputta) with faith must approach teachers and, having respectfully received their instructions, only then can it be known. Indeed, in the words of the Buddha, there appear various Pali methods that are the cause of confusion for the eye of wisdom of grammarians, in terms of word (sadda), meaning (attha), and intention (adhippāya).

Among those three (causes of confusion), this is the cause of confusion in terms of word (sadda): Where it should be said 'virattā kosiyāyanī,' the Feminine Nominative case is seen as 'viratte kosiyāyane.' Where it should be said 'ko puriso,' the Pronominal Nominative case is seen as 'ke purise.' Where it should be said 'kinnāmo te upajjhāyo,' a compound word (samāsa) in the Masculine sphere is seen as 'konāmo te upajjhāyo.' What name...
170:
"Konāmo" is an alutta-samāsa (a compound where the case ending is not dropped). Because it is made an alutta-samāsa, this method should also be understood: "What is the name of this woman? (konāmā itthī)" and "What is the name of this family? (konāmaṃ kulaṃ)." Where it should be said, "Great King, where is your army? (kva te balaṃ mahārājā)," it is found as "ko te balaṃ mahārājā." In this place, the word "ko" is seen with a Locative case ending, having a sound slightly similar to the word "kva." Indeed, the words "kva" and "ko" have sounds slightly similar to each other. Likewise, where it should be said, "I shall dwell here in Sāvatthī during the winter and summer months (idha hemantagimhesu)," it is found as "idha hemantagimhisu"; and where it should be said, "That fool cannot bind the benefit with that Dhamma (na tenatthaṃ abandhi so)," it is found as "na tenatthaṃ abandhisū." Other instances of confusion should also be applied in this manner.

This is the cause of confusion in terms of meaning (attha-sammuṭṭhāna): In this Pali verse, "Yaṃ na kañcanadvepiñcha, andhena tamasā gataṃ," the letter "na" should be connected with the word "kataṃ." "Na kataṃ" means "as if done (kataṃ viya)." Here, the word "na" is used in the sense of comparison (simile), not in the sense of negation (prohibition).

"The man who is free from blind faith (assaddho),
Who knows the unconditioned (Nibbāna) (akataññū),
Who has cut the connection to saṃsāra (sandhicchedo),
Who has destroyed the opportunity for rebirth (hatāvakāso),
And who has vomited out all desires (vantāso),
He is indeed the supreme man (uttamaporiso)."
Other such words should also be applied in this way.

This is the cause of confusion in terms of intention (adhippāya-sammuṭṭhāna): Although it should be said, "Having killed craving, the conceit 'I am,' the views of eternalism and annihilationism, and the delight and lust dependent on the twelve sense-bases, the Arahant (Brāhmaṇa) goes free from suffering," it was not said directly like that. Taking that same meaning, it was said by another figurative method (pariyāya):

"Having killed mother and father,
And two warrior kings,
Having destroyed a kingdom together with its inhabitants,
The Arahant goes free from suffering."
171:
“O monks, cut down the forest of defilements [with the Path-knowledge], do not cut down the tree. From the forest of defilements, fear [such as birth, etc.] arises. Having cut down both the forest of defilements that pulls one toward existence and the undergrowth of defilements that stands in the forest of unwholesome states, be those who are without the forest of defilements.” Other such passages should also be applied in this way. Thus, in the Word of the Buddha, various methods of Pāḷi are seen which serve as the ground for the confusion of the eye of wisdom of those who contemplate letters, whether by sound, by meaning, or by intention. In reference to this, it is said:

“Even those who know the entire science of grammar are confused in the sequence of the Pāḷi text,
For in the Pāḷi, there are mostly methods that differ from the methods of worldly ethics (Lokanīti).
Therefore, a wise person, having abandoned even the status of being a scholar in external subjects,
Should train only in this Piṭaka, which is the means of crossing the ocean of the stainless Dhamma that leads to the landing place of Nibbāna.”

Because the methods of Pāḷi are thus difficult to understand, the pure nominative case (paṭhamā vibhatti) of such terms as “vanappagumbe, bāle ca, paṇḍite ca,” etc., should be understood as the essential meaning. One should not take them as being in the locative (sattami) or accusative (dutiyā) case merely because of the similarity of sound. Although those terms have the same sound as the locative and accusative cases, they function as indicators of the nominative sense. Indeed, words with the same sound become indicators of specific meanings by virtue of the sense, the context, the gender, or the association with other words, and so forth. How is that? When it is said, “Sīho gāyati (Sīha sings),” the meaning is understood as “a man of such a name.” But when it is said, “Sīho naṅguṭṭhaṃ cāleti (The sīha wags its tail),” it is understood as “the king of beasts (a lion).” Thus, the specific meaning of words with the same sound is revealed by the power of the sense (function).

When it is said, “Sindhavamānehi (Bring the sindhava),” while standing on a battlefield, it is understood as “a horse.” However, when it is said, “Sindhavamānehi” in a hospital, it is understood as “Saindhava salt.” Thus, the specific meaning of words with the same sound is revealed by the power of the context (pakarana). When “issā” is said, it is understood as “the mental state of such a name (envy).” But when “isso” is said, it is understood as “a bear.” Thus, the specific meaning of words that are partially similar in sound is revealed by the power of gender.
172:
In such phrases as “one who carries a pot (ghaṭadhāraka), one who carries a staff (daṇḍadhāraka),” etc., although the pot, staff, etc., are marks (liṅga), they are not intended here because this is the domain of words with the same sound.

When it is said, “Envy (issā) arises,” and “Bears (issā) followed the man,” the specific meanings already mentioned are revealed by the power of association with other words (uppajjati, anubandhiṃsu) for the words “issā” which are identical in sound in every way. Likewise, when it is said, “Monks, the lion (sīha), the king of beasts, comes out from his lair in the evening,” it is understood as the kesara lion, the lord of beasts. But when it is said, “Sīha the novice, Sīha the general,” it is understood as “the novice named Sīha, the general named Sīha.” In this way, the specific meaning of words with the same sound is revealed by the power of association with other words.

In the sentence, “The monks of the group of six (chabbaggiyā bhikkhū) saw the monks of the group of seventeen (sattarasavaggiye bhikkhū) repairing the monastery,” the specific meanings known as the nominative (paccatta) and accusative (upayoga) of the words “bhikkhū,” which are identical in sound, are revealed by the power of association with other words (chabbaggiyā, sattarasavaggiye).

Likewise, in “Monk (bhikkhu), bale out this boat,” and “A certain monk (bhikkhu) said this to the Blessed One,” the specific meanings known as the vocative sense and the nominative sense of the words “bhikkhu,” which are identical in sound, are revealed by the power of association with other words (siñca, avoca). Therefore, although “vanappagumbe yathā phussitagge,” etc., are similar to the locative (bhumma) and accusative (upayoga) cases, they should be understood only as pure nominative (paccatta) cases by the power of association with other words.

Indeed, such forms occur like the locative and accusative cases only through the substitution of the letter ‘e’ for the nominative singular and plural. If it is asked, “Venerable sir, since such forms are found in the Pāḷi, should it not be said that there is also a masculine gender ending in ‘e’?” It should not be said so, because those forms are specific forms that are included within the status of ending in ‘o’. Since they are established by the power of substitution (ādesa), there is no separate masculine gender ending in ‘e’. Therefore, only the seven aforementioned varieties of masculine gender should be accepted.
173:
Some might say: "Taking this method of the word *Purisa*, the declension of all *o*-ending words like *bhūto, bhūtā, bhūtaṃ* is analyzed. In that declension, why are the forms with the substitution of *-āya* for the dative singular not mentioned?" (The answer is:) It is not mentioned to show the distinction. When carefully examining such dative singular forms in the Pāli method and the ancient commentary method, they are found briefly in only these four places, or in seven places in detail: "in the object of a verb of motion, in the object of a verb of leading, in the case transformation, and for the sake of that [action]." However, in general dative contexts such as giving, liking, bearing, and the use of *namo*, etc., the forms with the substitution of *-āya* are not found. Thus, to show this distinction, they are not mentioned.

In connection with the act of giving, the form with the substitution of *-āya* for the dative singular is seen in "A girl should be given to a handsome man" (*Abhirūpāya kaññā deyyā*). Therefore, should not forms like *purisāya, bhūtāya*, etc., be mentioned in this *Saddanīti* treatise? If so, why is it said that they are not found in general dative contexts like giving, liking, bearing, and the use of *namo*? It is because it is not the Pāli method. This method, "A girl should be given to a handsome man," comes from secular grammar (*Saddasattha*), not from the Buddha's word. When it comes to the Buddha's word, the word-form will be "A girl should be given to a handsome man" (*Abhirūpassa kaññā deyyā*).

"Venerable Sir, is it not true that the substitution of *-āya* for the dative singular is also seen in the use of *namo*, etc.? Even subtle scholars who move within the Dispensation pay homage to the Triple Gem by saying 'Namo Buddhāya,' etc. And some also [say]:

'Homage to the Buddha, homage to the Buddha.
Homage to the Dhamma, homage to the Buddha who possesses the Dhamma.
Homage to the Saṅgha, homage to the Saṅgha.
By this act of homage, may there be safety for me.'

'In the lake of the face, I constantly offer the lotuses of the eyes, which are well-blossomed, to the Buddha for the sake of worshipping the lotus of his feet.'

'A man asks a man for some object; a man sends a messenger to a man.' Do they not also make such verse compositions?"

It is true; scholars who move within the Dispensation do so. Even so, those scholars, by the power of the practice they have mastered in secular grammar, take the method from secular grammar and compose such verses and prose passages characterized by the substitution of *-āya*; they pay homage [to the Triple Gem]. There are children, at the very least, who have no practice in secular grammar; those children also, hearing the words of others...
174:
“In the lake of the face, I constantly offer the lotuses of the eyes, which are well-blossomed and petal-shaped, to the Buddha for the sake of worshipping the lotus of his feet.” And: “A man asks a man for some object; a messenger is sent for the sake of a man.” Do they not also make such verse compositions?

It is true; subtle scholars who move within the Dispensation pay homage to the Triple Gem by saying “Namo Buddhāya,” etc., and they also make verse compositions. Even so, those scholars, by the power of the practice they have mastered in secular grammar, take the method from secular grammar and compose such verses and prose passages characterized by the substitution of *-āya*; they pay homage to the Triple Gem by saying “Namo Buddhāya,” etc.

Even children, who at the very least have no practice in secular grammar, pay homage to the Triple Gem by saying “Namo Buddhāya,” etc., by the power of practice from hearing the words of others. Those who say “Namo Buddhassa” are very few. In some regions, teachers who teach literature to children teach “Namo Buddhāya” at the beginning of the alphabet, but they do not teach “Namo Buddhassa.”

Nevertheless, when examining the Pāli method and the ancient commentary method, except for the four places such as the object of a verb of motion, or the seven places in detail, the forms with the substitution of *-āya* for the dative singular are not found in any general dative context such as giving, liking, bearing, or connection with the word *namo*. Therefore, it should be understood that the words composed by some, such as “Namo Buddhāya” and “Buddhāya dānaṃ denti,” when they reach the Pāli [standard], become other forms like “Namo Buddhassa” and “Buddhassa dānaṃ denti.”

This is the composition of usage for the substitution of *-āya* in accordance with the Pāli method and the commentary method: “He goes to the Buddha for refuge” (*Buddhāya saraṇaṃ gacchati*) or “He goes to the Buddha for refuge” (*Buddhaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchati*); “They lead to the Buddha in the city” (*Buddhāya nagaraṃ nenti*) or “They lead to the Buddha in the city” (*Buddhaṃ nagaraṃ nenti*); “The Dhamma is honored for the Buddha” (*Buddhāya sakkato dhammo*) or “The Dhamma is honored by the Buddha” (*Buddhena sakkato dhammo*); “He renounces life for the Buddha” (*Buddhāya jīvitaṃ pariccajati*) or “He renounces life for the sake of the Buddha” (*Buddhassa atthāya jīvitaṃ pariccajati*); “The other sectarians depart from the Buddha” (*Buddhāya apenti aññatitthiyā*) or “The other sectarians depart from the Buddha” (*Buddhasmā apenti aññatitthiyā*)...
175:
Alternatively, except for these seven instances such as in the variations “buddhāya dhammatā, buddhassa dhammatā” or “buddhāya pasanno, buddhe pasanno,” the substitution of -āya is not seen elsewhere. Indeed, this is true—in the Pali text known as the Great Homage (Mahānamakkāra), which is cherished by the virtuous, the substitution of -āya is not seen in the dative case (sampadāna) when associated with the word 'namo'. In this context, the text “Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa” is called the Mahānamakkāra-pāṭha. In this Pali as well, the substitution of -āya is not seen. Also in the Vammika Sutta, it is said “Namo karohi nāgassa,” where the substitution of -āya is not seen. In the Ambaṭṭha Sutta as well, it is said “Sotthi bhadante hotu rañño, sotthi janapadassa” (May there be safety for the King, Venerable Kaṇha; may there be safety for the country); thus, the substitution of -āya is not seen.

Even in the explanation of the meaning of the text “suppabuddhaṃ,” the substitution of -āya is not seen in the dative case even when associated with the word 'namo'. Indeed, it is so—in the commentary on this Pali verse: “The disciples of Gotama always awaken happily; those whose mindfulness is constantly directed toward the Buddha by day and by night,” there is a specific grammatical arrangement that excludes the substitution of -āya, stating: “The son of a man with right view, while throwing dice, reflected on the recollection of the Buddha (buddhānussati) and threw the dice saying ‘Namo buddhassa’.” Likewise, in the commentary on the Dhanañjānī Sutta of the Sagāthāvagga, a specific grammatical arrangement excluding the substitution of -āya is seen: “Whether you are standing, sitting, sneezing, or coughing, you pay homage to that shaven-headed ascetic by saying ‘Namo buddhassa’.” Similarly, in various places, it is said: “He gives a gift to the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha (buddhappamukhassa bhikkhusaṅghassa)...”
176:
“Food is not pleasing to that man (he has indigestion).” “Truth is pleasing to the monk.” “He holds an umbrella for the Buddha.” “He praises the Buddha.” In such instances, a specific grammatical arrangement excluding the substitution of -āya is observed. Thus, in many dative contexts such as giving (dāna) and liking (rocana), the form of the dative singular with the substitution of -āya is not seen.

However, it is seen in four instances, such as the object of a verb of motion (gatyatthakamma). For example, in “mūlāya paṭikasseyya” (he should be pulled back to the beginning [of the offense]) and “appo saggāya gacchati” (few beings go to heaven), it is seen in the object of a verb of motion. Here, the meanings are “mūlaṃ paṭikasseyya” and “appo saggaṃ gacchati.” In the word “paṭikasseyya,” the root 'kasa' is used in the sense of motion; because it is qualified by the prefix 'pati', it means “ākaddheyya” (should pull). In the phrase “This man desires my welfare; he who, having seized me, leads me to the water (udakāya neti),” it is seen in the object of a verb of leading (nayanatthakamma). Here, the meaning is “he leads me to the water (udakaṃ neti), he makes me reach his own dwelling-pool.” In the phrase “Venerable sirs, desist from my words (mama vacanāya),” it is seen in the change of case (vibhatti-vipariṇāma). This is because the meaning is understood in the sense of the ablative (nissakka) as “desist from my words (mama vacanato).” In “The lord of my great flock of hamsas (mahāgaṇāya bhattā me),” it is also seen in the change of case. This is because the meaning is understood in the sense of possession (sāmi/genitive) as “the lord of my great flock of hamsas.” Here, the intended meaning is “my king of hamsas.” In “We are those who are not honored by King Dhanañjaya (dhanañjayāya),” it is also seen in the change of case. Here, the genitive case is used in the sense of the agent (kattar) as “We are those who are not honored by King Dhanañjaya.” Thus, although it should be said as “dhanañjayassa” or “dhanañjayena,” the dative case “dhanañjayāya” is used instead; since there is no dative context such as the act of giving, it is appropriate only as a change of case. Therefore, the meaning should be taken as “We are not honored or supported by King Dhanañjaya.” Other instances of case change should also be sought.
177:
However, thousands of word forms with the substitution of -āya, such as “virāgāya (for dispassion), upasamāya (for peace), nirodhāya (for cessation),” occur in that sense (tad-attha, i.e., 'for the purpose of'). Even the commentators, when explaining the meaning of the term 'Dhamma-Vinaya', used the word form with the substitution of -āya based on that sense of purpose (tad-attha), saying: “For the sake of disciplining the dhammas (dhammānaṃ vinayāya). For this Vinaya is for the benefit of faultless states, not for the benefit of existence or wealth, etc.” Thus, the forms of the dative singular with the substitution of -āya are evident only in these four instances: the object of a verb of motion, the object of a verb of leading, the change of case, and the sense of purpose (tad-attha). They do not occur in any other dative contexts such as giving (dāna) or liking (rocana). Indeed, in the Niruttipiṭaka, it is stated that “'atthāya' is a dative expression (sampadāna-vacana),” mentioning the word form with the substitution of -āya. However, such forms are not mentioned for words like 'purisa' (man), because such word forms do not occur in all dative contexts. Even in the Kaccāyana grammar, in the commentary (vutti) on the rule “āya catutthekavacanassa tu,” it is stated: “for the benefit (atthāya), for the welfare (hitāya), for the happiness (sukhāya) of gods and men.” It does not say “purisāya,” “samaṇāya,” or “brāhmaṇāya.”

Here, an objection (siyā) might arise: “Venerable sir, in the commentary on that very rule, it is asked: ‘Why say dative (catutthī)? To allow for purisassa mukhaṃ (the face of the man). Why say singular (ekavacanassa)? To allow for purisānaṃ dadāti (he gives to the men). Why say optionally (vā)? To allow for dātā hoti samaṇassa vā brāhmaṇassa vā (he is a giver to either a monk or a brahmin).’ Does this not show the word forms like ‘purisāya, samaṇāya, brāhmaṇāya’ by way of method? Is it not that ‘purisāya’ etc. are simply not formed when associated with the word ‘mukha’, or due to being plural, or due to the optionality, but they would certainly be formed in places free from such conditions as association with the word ‘mukha’?” To this objection, the following reply is given: “The one who says ‘Why say dative? To allow for purisassa mukhaṃ’ implies that if the substitution of -āya...”
178:
(The teacher Kaccāyana), wishing to show that "if (the substitution of -āya) occurs, it occurs only in the dative case (catutthī), not in the genitive case (chaṭṭhī)," showed the word "mukha." By showing this, he does not mean to show that "when a verbal word that is the object of the recipient (sampadāna), such as 'gives' (deti), exists in the place of the word 'mukha', the substitution of -āya occurs." Even when saying, "What is the purpose of the word 'ekavacana' (singular)? He gives to the men (purisānaṃ dadāti)," he is showing that "the substitution of -āya occurs only in the singular, not in the plural." He spoke this word "dadāti" (gives) to make known the dative (sampadāna) status of the word "purisānaṃ." He does not make known the meaning that "when a verbal word that is the object of the recipient, such as 'gives', exists, the substitution of -āya for the dative singular occurs." Even when saying, "What is the purpose of the word 'vā' (optionally)? He is a giver to a recluse or to a brahmin (samaṇassa vā brāhmaṇassa vā)," he makes it known that "the substitution of -āya occurs optionally only in the dative (sampadāna)." He does not make known the prescription of the substitution of -āya based on actions such as giving.

If the prescription of the substitution of -āya were based on actions such as giving, the author of the Vutti (commentary) should have said, in the very place of the primary examples in the commentary on the rule, "purisāya diyate" (it is given to the man) and so on, like the purpose-usages (tad-attha-payoga) "atthāya, hitāya." However, he did not say so. If one asks, "Why?" it is because such usage does not exist in the Buddha's words or in the ancient commentaries. Indeed, in the text of the Niruttipiṭaka, the Venerable Mahākaccāyana, who possessed the four analytical insights (paṭisambhidā), showed only forms devoid of the substitution of -āya, such as "purisassa diyate." And the Elder, while saying "'atthāya' is a dative expression (sampadāna-vacana)," pointed out only the form with the substitution of -āya for the dative singular, without regarding actions such as giving. Therefore, that usage is understood to be a purpose-usage (tad-attha-payoga). Thus, for these reasons, it should be understood that "the prescription of the substitution of -āya is not based on actions such as giving." If this is so, would only purpose-usages such as "atthāya, hitāya" be the scope of the rule "āya catutthekavacanassa tu," and not others? That is not so; others are also the scope of that rule. Which ones? "Mūlāya paṭikasseyya..."
179:
"...Only a few go to heaven (saggāya gacchati), he leads to the water (dakāya neti), Venerable sirs, refrain from my words (vicanāya), it is the alms-food of the group (gaṇāya bhattaṃ)," and so on. However, expressions such as "or by going to heaven (saggassa gamanena vā)" are not the scope because of the authority of the word "vā" (which implies optionality).

Venerable Sir, if this is so, the author of the Vutti, having said in the primary examples, "for the benefit, for the welfare, for the happiness of gods and humans," should also have said "mūlāya paṭikasseyya" and so on. Why is it said in the counter-example, "What is the purpose of the word 'vā'? Or by going to heaven (saggassa gamanena vā)"? It is true; there is a reason for not saying it. Listen to that reason. In this context of "mūlāya paṭikasseyya, appo saggāya gacchati," the words "mūlāya" and "saggāya" are not pure dative expressions (suddha-sampadāna) because they occur in the sense of the object of a verb of motion (gatyattha-kamma). Therefore, they were not mentioned in the primary examples.

Similarly, in the case of "he leads to the water (dakāya neti)," the word "dakāya" is not a pure dative expression because it occurs in the sense of the object of a verb of leading (nayanattha-kamma); thus it was not mentioned. In the case of "Venerable sirs, refrain from my words (vicanāya)," the word "vicanāya" occurs in the sense of the ablative (nissakka/pañcamī). In the case of "alms-food of the group (gaṇāya bhattaṃ)," the word "gaṇāya" occurs in the sense of the genitive (sāmi/chaṭṭhī). In the case of "not worshipped for Dhanañjaya (dhanañjayāya)," the word "dhanañjayāya" occurs in the sense of the genitive by way of the agent (kattū). Because these are not pure dative expressions, they were not mentioned.

In the counter-example as well, the word "saggassa" is not a pure dative expression because it stands near the word "gamana" (going) and occurs in the sense of the object of a verb of motion. Thus, it was not said as "What is the purpose of the word 'vā'? Or by going to heaven (saggassa gamanena vā)." Thus, in this matter, by the method mentioned, reaching the Buddha's words and the method of the ancient commentaries, the forms with the substitution of -āya for the dative singular are evident only in the four places such as the object of motion (gatyattha-kamma). It should be understood that it is not in any dative context such as giving (dāna) or pleasing (rocana).

Venerable Sir, because we see the form with the substitution of -āya for the dative singular in the usage of giving, such as "He gave the sandalwood essence to the eldest daughter (jeṭṭhikāya adāsi), he gave the golden garland to the younger sister (kaṇiṭṭhāya)," there should also be usages such as "given to the princess (rājakanyāya diyate)..."
180:
"...The ornament is pleasing to the princess (rājakanyāya ruccati), he holds the umbrella for the princess (rājakanyāya chattaṃ dhāreti), perform salutation to the princess (rājakanyāya namo karohi), may there be safety for the princess (rājakanyāya sotthi bhavatu), he praises the princess (rājakanyāya silāghate)." This being so, why do you say, "Reaching the words of the Buddha and the method of the ancient commentaries, the forms with the substitution of -āya for the dative singular are evident only in the four places such as the object of motion, and not in any dative context such as giving or pleasing"?

Sir, you have entered the wrong path; you do not understand the meaning of our words. Our meaning in this matter is this: All feminine nouns (itthiliṅga) in the singular are very similar in the third (instrumental), fourth (dative), fifth (ablative), sixth (genitive), and seventh (locative) case positions; the differences are few. Therefore, excluding those feminine nouns, for words such as 'purisa' and 'citta' in the masculine (pulliṅga) and neuter (napuṃsakaliṅga) genders which stand in their natural state ending in '-a' (akāranta-pakati), the forms with the substitution of -āya for the dative singular are not found in any dative context such as giving or pleasing in the Buddha's words and so on.

For that very reason, words such as "mūlāya, saggāya, dakāya, vacanāya, gaṇāya" are evident in the three places such as the object of motion, while hundreds of words in the three genders such as "abhiññāya, sambodhāya, nibbānāya" are evident in the fourth place, which is the sense of purpose (tad-attha). They are not evident in pure dative contexts such as "deti" (gives), "rocati" (pleases), and "dhāreti" (holds/bears). In this regard, there are these verses:

The form combined with the substitution of -āya
For the dative singular of non-feminine nouns
Stands in four places.

One should point them out as occurring in the object of motion,
In the object of the sense of leading,
In the substitution of cases (vibhatti-vipallāsa),
And in the sense of purpose (tad-attha).

"Mūlāya paṭikasseyya," "Appo saggāya gacchati."
Thus, in the object of motion, we have seen it in the Dispensation.
182: I shall now state the paradigm of noun declension (nāmika-padamālā): Satthā (the teacher), Satthā (the teachers), Satthāro (the teachers). Satthāraṃ (the teacher - acc.), Satthāro (the teachers - acc.). Satthārā (by the teacher), Satthārehi, Satthārebhi (by the teachers). Satthu, Satthussa, Satthuno (of the teacher), Satthānaṃ, Satthārānaṃ (of the teachers). Satthārā (from the teacher), Satthārehi, Satthārebhi (from the teachers). Satthu, Satthussa, Satthuno (of the teacher), Satthānaṃ, Satthārānaṃ (of the teachers). Satthari (in the teacher), Satthāresu (in the teachers). Bho Sattha, Bho Satthā (O teacher), Bhavanto Satthāro (O teachers). This is the method found in the Cūḷanirutti composed by the Elder Yamaka. Here, as well as in the Niruttipiṭaka and the Kaccāyana, the word "satthunā" should also be accepted even if it does not appear (in Cūḷanirutti), because it is found as "dhammarājena satthunā". The sequence "satthārā, satthunā, satthārehi, satthārebhi" should also be understood. Here, even if there is no difference in meaning, showing another word through the power of a specific consonant, or even if there is no specific consonant, through the power of a difference in meaning, is the method of Nirutti; therefore, it should be understood that the word "satthā" is mentioned twice as singular and plural. In the Niruttipiṭaka etc., the nominative plural "satthā" does not appear. Although it does not appear, because the nominative plural "avitakkitā" is seen in the Pali text "avitakkitā maccumupabbajanti", the status of the word "satthā" as a nominative plural must certainly be desired. Likewise, words like vattā, dhātā, gantā, etc., follow that same path. Similarly, in the Niruttipiṭaka, the accusative plural "satthāre" and the dative and genitive singular and plural "satthussa, satthānaṃ" appear, but they do not appear in the Cūḷanirutti. Among those forms, because of the findings "mātāpitaro poseti" and "bhātaro atikkamati", the accusative plural form "satthāre" seems inappropriate. In the Kaccāyana etc., two forms of the vocative singular, "bho sattha, bho satthā", are mentioned by way of short and long vowels. In the Niruttipiṭaka, the vocative singular "bho sattha" is mentioned by way of a short vowel, and the vocative plural "bhavanto satthāro" is mentioned by way of the āra-substitution.
183: In the Cūḷanirutti, the vocative singular "bho sattha" is mentioned by way of a short vowel, and the vocative plural "bho satthā" is mentioned by way of a long vowel. All this should be examined in the scriptures and accepted in a way that is not contradictory. Now, I shall show the specific form of the word "satthu" that we have seen. Namely, in the Pali text "imesaṃ mahānāma tiṇṇaṃ satthūnaṃ ekā niṭṭhā udāhu puthu niṭṭhā", the word "satthūnaṃ" is found; therefore, this sequence should also be known: "satthu, satthussa, satthuno, satthānaṃ, satthārānaṃ, satthūnaṃ". Abhibhavitā (the overcomer), Abhibhavitā (the overcomers), Abhibhavitāro (the overcomers). Abhibhavitāraṃ (the overcomer - acc.), Abhibhavitāro (the overcomers - acc.). Abhibhavitārā, Abhibhavitunā (by the overcomer), Abhibhavitārehi, Abhibhavitārebhi (by the overcomers). Abhibhavitu, Abhibhavitussa, Abhibhavituno (of the overcomer), Abhibhavitānaṃ, Abhibhavitārānaṃ, Abhibhavitūnaṃ (of the overcomers). Abhibhavitārā (from the overcomer), Abhibhavitārehi, Abhibhavitārebhi (from the overcomers). Abhibhavitu, Abhibhavitussa, Abhibhavituno (of the overcomer), Abhibhavitānaṃ, Abhibhavitārānaṃ (of the overcomers). Abhibhavitari (in the overcomer), Abhibhavitāresu (in the overcomers). Bho Abhibhavita, Bho Abhibhavitā (O overcomer), Bhavanto Abhibhavitāro (O overcomers). Just as the paradigm of declension for the original form "abhibhavitu" is applied here according to the method of "satthu", so also the paradigm of declension for "paribhavitu" and others, and other similar words, should be applied according to the method of "satthu". Here, other similar names are the original forms such as "vattu, dhātu" etc., of the words "vattā, dhātā" etc. Vattā (speaker), dhātā (bearer), gantā (goer), netā (leader), dātā (giver), kattā (doer), cettā (accumulator), tātā (protector). Chettā (cutter), bhettā (breaker), hantā (killer), metā (measurer), jetā (conqueror), boddhā (knower), ñātā (knower), sotā (hearer). Gajjitā (roarer), vassitā (warbler/shouter), bhattā (devotee/servant), mucchitā (one who is infatuated), paṭisedhitā (prohibitor). Bhāsitā (speaker), pucchitā (questioner), khantā (forbearer), uṭṭhātā (striver), okkamitā (descender), tatā (spreader).
184:
Words such as nattā (grandson), panattā (great-grandson), akkhātā (speaker), sahitā (one who endures), paṭisevitā (one who associates), netā (leader), and vinetā (discipliner) occur in the sense of the pure agent (suddhakattu). Other words such as uppādetā (producer), viññāpetā (informer), sandassetā (one who demonstrates), pabrūhetā (one who increases), and bodhetā (one who awakens) should be understood as existing in the sense of the causal agent (hetukattu). However, these words—kattā, khattā, nettā, bhattā, pitā, and bhātā—differ slightly in the Sutta (from the word satthu); I shall explain that distinction. Among words such as satthā, some always occur in conjunction with the accusative (dutiyā) and genitive (chaṭṭhī) cases, while some occur without such conjunction. Among those words, kattā and others differ slightly from the word satthu by virtue of morphological variation. 

To illustrate this variation: in the passage "Uṭṭhehi katte taramāno, gantvā vessantaraṃ vada" (Arise, O minister, in haste; go and speak to Vessantara), the word "katte" is the vocative singular form. Thus, it is a morphological variation from the form "bho kattā." In the passage "Tena hi bho khatte yena campeyyakā brāhmaṇagahapatikā tenupasaṅkama" (Therefore, O minister, approach the place where the brahmins and householders of Campā are), the word "khatte" is also the vocative singular form. This too is a morphological variation from the form "bho khattā." In the passage "Nette ujuṃ gate sati" (When the eye has gone straight), the word "nette" is the locative singular form. This is a morphological variation from the form "nettari." In the passage "Ārādhayati rājānaṃ, pūjaṃ labhati bhattūsu" (He pleases the king and receives honor among the lords), the word "bhattūsu" is the locative plural form. It is a morphological variation from the form "bhattāresu." Because "bhattūsu" is seen here, and "pitūsu" is seen in the passage "mātāpitūsu paṇḍitā" (the wise towards parents), the same method should be understood for words such as vattūsu, dhātūsu, gantūsu, netūsu, dātūsu, and kattūsu. It appears to us that this method is also desired for the word satthu. 

Pitā, pitā, pitaro (Nominative). Pitaraṃ, pitaro (Accusative). Pitarā, pitunā, petyā, pitarehi, pitarebhi, pitūhi, pitūbi (Instrumental). Pitu, pitussa,
185:
Pituno, pitānaṃ, pitarānaṃ, pitūnaṃ (Genitive). Pitarā, petyā, pitarehi, pitarebhi, pitūhi, pitūbi (Ablative). Pitu, pitussa, pituno, pitānaṃ, pitarānaṃ, pitūnaṃ (Dative). Pitari, pitaresu, pitūsu (Locative). Bho pita, bho pitā, bhavanto pitaro (Vocative). In this paradigm, the declension of the word bhātu (brother) should also be applied, excluding these two forms: "petyā" and "pitūnaṃ." In that regard, because of the occurrences "mātyā ca petyā ca kataṃ susādhu" (what is done by mother and father is very good), "anuññātosi mātāpitūhi" (you are permitted by parents), and "mātāpitūnaṃ accayena" (by the passing of parents), the morphological variations of the word pitu such as "petyā, pitūhi, pitūbhi, pitūnaṃ," as well as the shortening of the vowel in "pitaro" etc., are distinctions from the word satthu. Among those variations, the form "petyā" should be understood as an irregular masculine form, similar to the words jantuyo, hetuyo, hetuyā, and adhipatiyā. 

Here, there is an objection and a clarification: You say that "words such as satthā and pitā are ākāranta (ending in -ā) based on their finished form, and they are ukāranta (ending in -u) based on their initial base form." If so, how do you explain the forms such as "satthāra" in passages like "hetu satthāradassanaṃ," "amātāpitarasaṃvaḍḍho" (one not raised by parents), and "kattāraniddesa"? We say that those words are also ukāranta based on their base form. "O teacher, are those words not ākāranta (ending in -a)?" No, they are indeed ukāranta. "O teacher, since the case endings such as yo, aṃ, and nā—which could cause the end of ukāranta words to be substituted with 'āra'—are not seen, should they not be ākāranta?" No, because in such a position, there is no occasion for the subsequent case endings like yo, aṃ, and nā. This is because this is the domain of compounds (samāsa). In the domain of compounds, even irregular forms are often seen. "O teacher, even if that is so, since the Niddesa Pali shows 'satthārato satthāraṃ gacchati' in a non-compound context, similar to the usage 'gāmato nikkhamati' (he leaves from the village)..."
186:
...should the words such as satthāra in "hetu satthāradassanaṃ" etc., be considered as ākāranta (ending in -a)? They should not be so considered. Even in the expression "satthārato satthāraṃ gacchati," it is ukāranta. For in this word (satthārato), although it is not a compound, the vowel 'u' of the word satthu receives the substitution of 'āra' (āra-ādesa) due to the suffix -to. Those case endings such as yo, aṃ, and nā, which you desire as the cause for the 'āra' substitution of the vowel 'u', are not the only criteria for the wise in such a position. 

If one asks, "What then are the criteria?" In a non-compound context, the suffix -to; in a compound context, the subsequent words; and in the absence of a subsequent word, the case endings starting with 'si'—these alone are the absolute criteria in such a position. To demonstrate this, in the commentary on the Dhammapada verse, "Yāvadeva anatthāya, ñattaṃ bālassa jāyati" (The knowledge of a fool is only for his ruin), the explanation of the meaning states: "Ayaṃ nimmātāpitaro..." (This person is one without parents; there is no punishment even if he is beaten). Here, because the word "nimmātāpitaro" is in the domain of a compound, when the 'si' suffix follows, the vowel 'u' receives the substitution of 'āra'; thereafter, by substituting the 'si' suffix with 'o', this word is ukāranta by its original nature. Based on its finished state, it also becomes okāranta (ending in -o), like the words "puriso" and "urago."

The analysis of the compound (samāsa-viggaha) here is: "Mātā ca pitā ca mātāpitaro (Mother and father are parents); etassa mātāpitaro natthi (To him, there are no parents); iti nimmātāpitaro (Thus, he is one without parents)." While existing as "nimmātāpitu" in its base form, the 'u' becomes 'āra' when the 'si' suffix follows. In some manuscripts of the Dhammapada Commentary, the reading "ayaṃ nimmātāpitiko" is found; we believe this was established by those who considered the word "ayaṃ nimmātāpitaro" to be inappropriate. That original commentary text is not inappropriate. For it agrees with the usage of the 'āra' substitution due to the 'si' suffix in the word "ekapitaro" in the Ummaṅga Jātaka Commentary. To demonstrate that—
187:
“O King of Videha, most noble among all chariot-riding kings, just like a biological brother, born of the same womb and having the same mother, so too should you love (and look upon) Prince Pañcālacanda.”

Teachers who are well-versed in the methods of Pali, when explaining the meaning of this Pali verse, stated: “Niyako means a biological brother of the same lineage, born of the same father and the same mother,” thus establishing the usage of the āra-substitution due to the si-suffix (nominative case). We see this āra-substitution due to the si-suffix not only in the masculine gender but also in the feminine gender within the Dispensation. For instance, in the Cullavagga of the Vinaya Piṭaka, the phrase “Assamaṇī hoti asakyadhītarā” (She who is not a Sakyan daughter is no longer a bhikkhunī) is found.

In this context, the compound analysis (samāsa-viggraha) is: “Because she is born in the Sakyan clan, she is the daughter of the Blessed One who is a Sakyan, thus she is called Sakyadhītarā; one who is not a Sakyan daughter is Asakyadhītarā.” Here too, when the si-suffix follows, the vowel ‘u’ is substituted with ‘āra’. Since the feminine gender is intended, the suffix ‘ā’ is added, and then the si-suffix is elided. In this way, when it becomes a compound word, some special forms are seen which differ from the declension patterns (nāmika-padamālā) of the words Satthu, Pitu, and Kattu. Other special forms should also be sought in the Suttantas by those who know the method. For who is capable of extracting and showing all the jewel-like word-forms that are interspersed and diverse within the ocean of the Buddha’s words, which cause wonder in the hearts of wise men? Therefore, we have shown only a small portion.

A wise person of quick intellect in this world,
Who constantly strives in the Teacher’s Pali,
Will have no doubt regarding the Pali.

Among the words we have presented here, such as “Satthā, Abhibhavitā, Vattā, Kattā,” etc., some words like “Pucchitā, Okkhamitā,” etc., always occur with the accusative case (upayogavacana). For instance—
188:
“Great King, do you remember having asked other recluses and brahmins this question? (Do you remember) having fallen into sleep?” Many such usages are seen. Some words (ending in the tu-suffix) such as “Abhibhavitā” (one who overcomes) and “Vattā” (one who speaks) always occur in conjunction with the genitive case (sāmivacana). Likewise, many usages are seen such as: “The overcomer of enemies; there are those who speak (reproachfully) of him. The giver of the Deathless (Nibbāna). The endurer of dangers. The Supreme Man who causes the unarisen Path to arise.” However, some words do not occur even with the accusative case (upayogavacana) because they always function as designations (paññatti). These are words like “Satthā” (Teacher), “Pitā” (Father), “Bhātā” (Brother), “Nattā” (Grandson), etc. In this context, the statement “always occur in conjunction with the accusative case” should be understood as referring to the sense of the object (kamma).

Having understood the occurrence of these ā-ending words which have an original u-ending base, those who desire proficiency in words and their meanings should further distinguish the meanings of the words, the declension of the original forms, and the similarities or differences between the words by categorizing them into three types based on gender and ending: “Satthā, Sattho, Satthaṃ.” Among these three, the word “Satthā” first stands in the original u-ending base and later becomes a masculine ā-ending word. The word “Sattho” first stands in the original a-ending base and later becomes a masculine o-ending word. The word “Satthaṃ” first stands in the original a-ending base and later becomes a neuter niggahīta-ending word. Among these three, “Satthā” is so called because he instructs and admonishes the world including the devas. Who is he? He is the Blessed One. “Sattho” is so called because it exists with wealth (attha); it is a group of people who have taken capital and gone to another region for trade. “Satthaṃ” is so called because meanings are shown and taught by means of this work; it refers to treatises such as Grammar. Alternatively, “Satthaṃ” is so called because beings are harmed or killed by this instrument; it refers to weapons like swords. As previously mentioned, “Satthā, Satthā, Satthāro. Satthāraṃ, Satthāro”...
189:
The declension (padamālā) should be formed as previously mentioned. For “Sattho, Satthā. Satthaṃ, Satthe,” the declension follows the masculine method (purisanaya). For “Satthaṃ, Satthāni, Satthā. Satthaṃ, Satthāni, Satthe,” the declension should be applied according to the method of the word ‘Citta’ in the neuter gender. Thus, in these three different types of declensions, the similarities and differences of the words must be distinguished.

The All-Knowing Teacher (Satthā) remains; the merchants (satthā) desiring wealth depart.
The man avoids the weapon (satthā); O merchants (satthā), give me wealth.

In this way, similarity occurs by mere commonality of sound (sutisamāñña).

The weapon (satthaṃ) which is sharp; with that sharp weapon,
The merchant (sattho), having made the fruit allowable (kappiya), offers it to the Teacher (Satthu).
The Teacher (Satthā) partakes of that fruit.

In this way, difference occurs by the power of non-commonality of sound (asutisamāñña), as well as by the power of gender and the final consonant. By forming pairs such as “Cetā, Ceto” and “Tātā, Tāto,” one should distinguish the meanings of the words, the declension of the original forms, and the similarities and differences of the words.

Among those words, “Cetā” first stands in the original u-ending base and later becomes a masculine ā-ending word; the word “Tātā” is the same. The word “Ceto” first stands in the original a-ending base and later becomes a masculine o-ending word; the word “Tāto” is the same. Among them, “Cetā” is so called because he collects or makes a pile; it means a person who builds a wall, a bricklayer. “Ceto” refers to the mind (citta), or a hunter of that name. Here, the mind is called “Ceto” by virtue of the meaning “cetayati cinteti—it thinks”; the hunter is called “Ceto” by virtue of designation (paññatti). “Tātā” is so called because he protects. “Aghassa tātā hitassa vidhātā—Protector from danger, provider of welfare” is its usage. In the word “Tāto” as well, it is called “Tāto” because he protects; it is used by sons toward fathers, by fathers toward sons, and toward other dear persons...
190:
This is a conventional expression used in common speech. The usage of the word 'tāta' (dear/father/son) should be understood in sentences such as: "That lonely father, dear one, will surely weep for a long time in the hermitage. The wealth acquired with great difficulty (by blowing the conch), the father has destroyed by blowing (the conch). Come, dear one." 

"Ceta, cetā, cetāro; cetāraṃ, cetāro"—this is the paradigm (padamālā) according to the Satthu-naya (the method of the word 'Satthu'). "Ceto, cetā; cetaṃ, cete; cetasā, cetenā"—this should be understood according to the Manogaṇa-naya (the method of the 'Mano' group). This is the nominal paradigm of the word 'ceta' when it signifies the mind (citta). "Ceto, cetā; cetaṃ, cete; cetenā"—this should be understood according to the Purisa-naya (the method of the word 'Purisa'). This is the nominal paradigm of the word 'ceta' when it signifies a designation (paññatti). 

"Tātā, tātā, tātāro; tātāraṃ"—this should be understood by the Satthu-naya. "Tāto, tātā, tātaṃ"—this should be understood by the Purisa-naya. In this way, in these nominal paradigms, the similarity and dissimilarity of the words should be determined. Likewise, by making a group of four based on gender and ending (anta) as "ñātā, ñāto, ñātaṃ, ñātā," one should determine the meaning of the words, the nominal paradigm of the original form, and the similarity and dissimilarity of the words.

Among those words, "ñātā" is a masculine form that first exists in the original u-kāranta (ending in u) and later becomes ā-kāranta (ending in ā). "Ñāto" and "ñātaṃ" are respectively masculine and neuter forms in the expressed genders, which first exist in the original a-kāranta and later become forms ending in 'o' and the niggahīta (ṃ). Indeed, their usages are seen as: "ñāto attho sukhāvaho" (a known meaning brings happiness) and "ñātametaṃ kuraṅgassa" (this is known by the deer). However, this word "ñātā" is a feminine form in the expressed genders, which first exists in the original ā-kāranta and remains ā-kāranta afterwards. Thus, there is the usage: "esā itthimayā ñātā" (this woman is known by me). Among those, on the masculine side, the meaning should be taken by the power of the active voice (kattukāraka) in the present tense as: "one knows, therefore he is a ñātā (knower)." On the side of the feminine and others, "it was known, therefore ñātā..."
191:
In the words "ñāto" and "ñātaṃ," the meaning should be taken by the power of the passive voice (kammakāraka) in the past tense. This method should be observed in other places as well, as applicable. The words "ñātā, ñātā, ñātāro, ñātāraṃ" should be understood by the method of the word 'Satthu'. The words "ñāto, ñātā, ñātaṃ" should be understood by the method of the word 'Purisa'. The words "ñātaṃ, ñātāni, ñātā, ñātaṃ, ñātāni, ñāte" should be understood by the method of the word 'Citta', which will be mentioned later. The words "ñātā, ñātā, ñātāyo, ñātaṃ, ñātā, ñātāyo" should be understood by the method of the word 'Kaññā', which will be mentioned later. In this way, in these nominal paradigms, the similarity and dissimilarity of the words should be determined. In other places too, similarity and dissimilarity should be investigated by this method as appropriate. The etymologies (nibbacana) of words such as vattā, dhātā, gantā, etc., should be understood as applicable, such as: "one who speaks is called vattā," "one who bears is called dhātā," "one who goes is called gantā."

Regarding the miscellaneous remarks we have made here, it should not be said that "this was spoken in an inappropriate place." Because this treatise called Saddanīti is undertaken for the purpose of manifesting the suitability and unsuitability of words and meanings; therefore, it is only beautiful when it is spoken by thoroughly stirring up the entire Māgadha language (Pali) in various ways, and not otherwise. Thus, because the desire to speak in various ways is possible, it should not be said that "this was spoken in an inappropriate place." Furthermore, because it is undertaken for the purpose of informing the wise through various means, the fault of repetition (punaruttidosa) should not be considered here. On the contrary, this Saddanīti should be respectfully learned by sons of good family endowed with faith for the sake of assisting the three Pitakas.

Thus, the words such as vattā, dhātā, gantā, which are similar to the word 'abhibhavitā', have been shown. Now, we shall show those that are dissimilar to that word. They are as follows:

Guṇavā gaṇavā ceva, balavā yasavā tathā.
Dhanavā sutavā vidvā, dhutavā katavāpi ca.
192:
The Blessed One (Bhagavā) is one who has welfare, one who has glory, one who has steadfastness, and one who has strength. Likewise, words such as one who has effort (yatavā), one who has generosity (cāgavā), and one who has snow (himavā) should be understood. After masculine and neuter words ending in 'a' (a-kāranta), the suffix 'vantu' usually follows. Those words ending in the vantu-suffix are guṇavā and so on. Because of seeing such forms as one who has perception (saññāvā), one who has rays (rassmivā), one who has a beard (massuvā), and one who has attendants (yasassivā), it should be shown that this vantu-suffix occurs in some places after words ending in 'ā', 'i', and 'u' in the feminine gender and so forth.

One who has mindfulness (satimā), one who has wisdom (gatimā), one who habitually sees the meaning (atthadassimā), one who has steadfastness (dhitimā), one who has wisdom (mutimā), one who has wisdom (matimā), one who has radiance (jutimā), one who has shame (hirimā), one who has praise (thutimā), one who has delight (ratimā), one who has restraint or a monk or effort (yatimā), one who has strength (balimā); likewise, one who has scratching or writing (kasimā), one who has a needle or purity (sucimā), one who has wisdom (dhīmā), one who has beauty (rucimā), one who has eyes (cakkhumā), one who has relatives (bandhumā), one who has a cause (hetumā), the venerable one (āyasmā), one who has a banner (ketumā), one who has Rahu (rāhumā); likewise, one who has a stump (khāṇumā), one who has radiance (bhāṇumā), one who has cattle (gomā), one who has lightning (vijjumā), one who has wealth (vasumā), and so on. Also, the Evil One who has demerit (pāpimā), one who has a son (puttimā), and the moon-god who has a moon-mansion (candimā) occur. These should be understood by the wise as words dissimilar to 'abhibhavitā'. After the letters 'i', 'u', and 'o', the suffix 'mantu' should follow. After words ending in 'ā' and 'i', it should be understood that the suffix 'imantu' occurs.

Guṇavā, guṇavā, guṇavanto. Guṇavantaṃ, guṇavante. Guṇavatā, guṇavantena, guṇavantehi, guṇavantebhi. Guṇavato, guṇavantassa, guṇavataṃ, guṇavantānaṃ. Guṇavatā, guṇavantā, guṇavantasmā, guṇavantamhā, guṇavantehi, guṇavantebhi. Guṇavato, guṇavantassa, guṇavataṃ, guṇavantānaṃ. Guṇavati, guṇavante, guṇavantasmiṃ, guṇavantamhi, guṇavantesu. O virtuous one! O virtuous ones! O virtuous ones!
193:
In this context, because the nominative plural forms "sīlavā" and "cakkhumā" are found in the Pāḷi texts, such as: "Come, friends, be virtuous (sīlavā)," and "Those who have gone under the influence of women, though strong, become weak; though powerful, they decline; though possessing vision (cakkhumā), they become blind," the plural form is used for "guṇavā" in the nominative and vocative positions. The same method applies to "guṇavā," "satimā," and so on.

In the Cūḷanirutti, the nominative plural and vocative plural forms appear as "guṇavā." However, in the Niruttipiṭaka, it appears only as the nominative singular. In both the Cūḷanirutti and the Niruttipiṭaka, the vocative singular appears as "bho guṇava" with a short vowel (rassa).

We, however, observe the long vowel (dīgha) form of the vocative singular "bhagavā" in hundreds of passages such as: "Indeed, O Blessed One (bhagavā), the factors of enlightenment (are good)," and "O Blessed One (bhagavā), how is it that a disciple is delighted in your teaching?" Therefore, in the case of the -vantu suffix, we consider it more appropriate to use the long vowel form, such as "bho guṇavā."

In the case of the -mantu and -imantu suffixes, because the short vowel (rassa) form of the vocative singular is seen in Pāḷi passages such as "cakkhuma" in "O you who have transcended all enmity and fear, I pay homage to your feet, O Visionary (cakkhuma)" and "Know thus, O Evil One (pāpima)," we consider it more appropriate to use the short vowel form, such as "bho satima" and "bho gatima."

Alternatively, since the vocative singular is stated with a long vowel as "āyasmā tissa" in the Commentary on the Mahāparinibbāna Sutta, one should apply the -mantu suffix method to the -vantu suffix and vice versa, except for the specific words stated with long vowels like "bhagavā" and "āyasmā." Thus, in texts like Kaccāyana, three types of vocative singular are stated—using the niggahīta, the short vowel, and the long vowel—as "bho guṇavaṃ, bho guṇava, bho guṇavā." By this method, forms such as "bho satimaṃ, bho satima, bho satimā" should also be understood.
194:
In the nominative plural position, three forms are stated: "guṇavanto, guṇavantā, guṇavanti." By these forms, the method for "satimanto, satimantā, satimanti," etc., is also shown. Among those forms, "bho guṇavaṃ, bho satimaṃ, guṇavantā, guṇavanti" and other such words are not well-known in the Pāḷi texts, unlike the well-known word "āyasmantā."
